projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Frank Pipperata was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: This is William Unger. It is May 30th. I am interviewing Frank Pipperata. All right. My first question is when did you join the Army and why?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: I joined the enlisted reserve, because World War II was just starting. I knew I was going to be drafted eventually, and they were offering a training program. So I joined -- I joined the enlisted reserved, went to school for six months of Army training, three months of radio repair and three months in Rutgers University was a pre-radar course. And when I finished that training, then I was called into active duty.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: What were the feelings of your friends and family when they realized you were going to sign up to join the Army?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, nobody really cared that -- that you really wanted to go. You -- you had to go. It wasn't a choice, so they accepted it. They weren't happy about it, but it was just accepted. And, of course, some people like tried to get jobs and dodged the draft and stuff like that, but there weren't too many of them.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: Did you have -- explain in detail your basic training and any other training that you had before you joined active duty.

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, as I said before, I went to six months' training before I went into active duty. Then when I went on active duty, I went to Port Monmouth and sort of repeated a lot of the training. I went to a radio repair course when I was on active duty also for about eight months. So I was well versed in electronics at that time.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: What was it like going through basic training? How did -- how did the -- the instructors treat you? What was the schooling like? How would you feel when you go -- when you were going through it?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, basic training was tough, because it wasn't like civilian life. You weren't used to getting up early and training and all that, but you went through it. One disturbing thing I had in my basic training, I was in just the -- a couple weeks, and I hit my 21st birthday. So they get you up about 5:00 o'clock to go to breakfast, and then you go to training courses. And it was about 10:00 o'clock in the morning before I even realized it was my 21st birthday. So I was highly irritated, because if I was home, it would be a big celebration. And there I had thousands of people; nobody knew it was my birthday, not even me.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: After basic training, when you were on active duty, where were you first deployed and what was your job there?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: After I finished my training, I went to a replacement depot, which is where you stay until somebody calls for your specific job training. And so I -- I was in the replacement depot in the States for a while. And then we went overseas to England, and I was in the replacement depot for a few months there. They had the invasion, went into France, and I went into France after the invasion. And it was after that that I was finally placed in an ordnance radio repair company. I was in the signal corps. So I was in the radio repair company, which we -- our job was to install radios in tanks and half-tracks and maintain communications in those units.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: England, that was -- was that your first time outside of the United States?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Yes. I was in central England, and I -- around a town named Chester, I believe, stayed several months there before I went into France.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: What was it like leaving the United States and everybody to go to England, and what did you feel like? What was your feelings when you got into England?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, it wasn't very nice, and our accommodations weren't good. They had us in what he they called Quonset huts, which was just a concrete floor and a metal shell. And they wouldn't put the heat on until late in the season. And it was very cold, very uncomfortable. I remember feeling hungry and cold. It -- it wasn't a pleasant situation at all.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: In France, where did you go in France and like what cities did you see?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, we didn't see many cities. When we went into France, we slept in pup tents in the fields someplace, which was very uncomfortable. The first two weeks I was in France, it rained every day for a two-week period, with the exception of the two Sundays. The two Sundays it cleared up. So we were in mud and wet. It -- it wasn't -- the first two weeks in France was not fun. Occasionally, we -- we would get to a city, pass through a city, and not -- we didn't see many cities in France until the war was over. And then I went to visit several cities.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: When you're in the cities during the war, did you see many people? And if you did, what were they like?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, you would see people -- we were in Army headquarters, so we -- so we went through -- half of the fighting men went through, and, of course, the cities were all bombed out. You would see people like just shuffling around, not -- not a pleasant sight. Occasionally, you'd see dead bodies around, people ignoring them. It -- it was very depressing.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: How did the people, the civilians, react when they saw American or Allied troops?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, when we went through the cities, if we were traveling in convoy, we were well received. But the men that originally went into the initial phases into France that were -- when they had the invasion, there was a little bad feeling there, because the German troops had been stationed in those areas for a long time, and they became friendly with the local people. Some of them intermarried. So, initially, you might get like some bad feeling. But then, generally, when you went through the towns, it was good. People welcomed you and were mostly friendly.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: Did you have any interesting experiences that you would like to tell about while you were in France during the war?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, it was just the -- occasionally, we were in dangerous spots. And when we were billeted, they had buzz bombs that would come over periodically, and so you were in a little danger. It -- it wasn't pleasant. You actually didn't know what was going to happen at any time.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: What is a buzz bomb? What does it do and what exactly is it like and stuff like that?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, these -- these buzz bombs, they had -- they would just fly over, and you would hear them. As long as you would hear the motor, people would ignore them. But then they were either timed to run out of fuel or the motor would stop, I don't know how it did, but then when it would stop, it would just glide down and explode. So you -- until -- while the motor was running, you weren't in any danger. When the motor stopped, then you had to see whether it was going to fall near where you are or not. So you would be going about your work. And as I say, when the motor was running, people would ignore them. When the motor would stop, everybody would stop.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: After France, did you go to anywhere else during the war?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: We were in Belgium for a while, Liege, Belgium, went from France to Belgium. And then later on, we were in Germany, near the Battle of the Bulge. I wasn't involved in there, but I was in the forward part of the advance part of the river. If they had succeeded in coming to the river, the Germans succeeding in coming to the river, I would have been in enemy territory. But, luckily, we won that Battle of the Bulge. It was very cold and snowy. It was -- it was a rough, rough time.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: While you were in Germany, what was it like being in Germany while the war was still going on? And after the war -- after the war ended and you were in there, what exactly did you do?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, we just maintained regular duties. As I say, the -- the buildings were bombed out. You know, it was a -- they took a lot of bombing, and so it was -- a lot of buildings were destroyed. And we would go into a big factory and set up billets and live there and just go about our duties. And you would see occasionally civilians -- a few civilians, but not the -- not many people around for us to deal with. Occasionally, maybe you might find somebody we'd buy something from or something like that, but not too many people.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: How did the very few civilians, German civilians that you met, how did -- did they treat you when they saw you? What was their general reaction after they -- after they lost?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, their attitude, losing the war, they were not in the best frame of mind. We came in contact with German prisoners that we used to work on the base and stuff like that, and they were cooperative. Well, they had to be. And, of course, they weren't mistreated in any way. And it was just -- they -- even the German prisoners of war conducted themselves in a -- in a military manner and even more than the GIs, because GIs were just civilian soldiers, and Germans were a little -- were a little more militant. But there was no -- we didn't have any problem with the German prisoners or civilians, either one. You would like stand guard duty in certain areas before the war was over, and you'd have to -- people going to work, you'd have to ask them for identification and things like that, but I'd never had any trouble with them.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: When the war ended, where were you exactly? And what did you feel and what did your comrades feel when you heard about it?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, when the war in Germany start -- stopped, I was overseas, I guess, over a year, a year and a half, and they were going to send us straight to the Pacific Theater of Operations, without going home to the States. So I was very unhappy about that. So we -- they sent us down to southern France. We got all shots, malaria shots and stuff like that, to go to the Pacific. And while we were in the process of doing that, they dropped those atom bombs, and the war stopped in Japan. And so I was very happy then the war was over. We were going home. And I was happy when they dropped those atom bombs. Although it caused a lot of deaths, there would have been a lot more deaths if you had to continue the war in the Pacific and attack the mainland of Japan. There would have been much more loss of life.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: What was your scariest moment, the moment -- the moment you were most afraid of overall during the war?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: I -- I don't think it was any one moment. You were exposed ...

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: Okay. Hold on. Did you ever personally see combat a during -- during your tours of -- during your tour of duty?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: No, I never was exposed to combat. We were in Army headquarters. The fighting troops went through before us, and then we were -- we followed them in.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: Did you make many friends during the -- during the war?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Yeah, I made quite a few good friends in the company I finally settled down. There was even a guy from my hometown. But I never continued any of those friendships after the war. I visited a couple guys after the war down South that I had served with, but never maintained any friendships.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: So -- so you really didn't keep in touch with the people that you met?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: No, I didn't.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: All right. What was your most -- between the -- the end of the war and when you went home, what was the most memorable -- memorable experience, good or bad?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, after the war, you had to wait for a point system to go back to the States. So I -- I wasn't married or I didn't have a girl friend or anything, so I wasn't in a hurry to get back once the war was start -- stopped. So they would ask if you wanted to go on leave and make trips around Europe. So I went on a week's leave in Switzerland, and I went to a -- a week's leave in the French Riviera, and I made a couple of trips to Paris and Belgium. So I -- I went on a few trips before I went home, when I finally went home in January of 1946.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: What was it like visiting all those places that people mostly -- that right now dream about going? How did you feel being able to do all that?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, it was a good experience, the travel, to see those cities, and the people were friendly, and the war was over. So it was a good -- it was a good thing.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: When you finally were able to go home, how did you feel and when were you exactly allowed to return to the United States?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, naturally, I was glad to get back to the States, and I was released from the Army almost immediately, just a matter of a couple weeks. And I didn't tell anybody I was coming home, because I didn't want a big party or anything. So I just surprised the family and come home one day -- one night, and it was January of '46.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: When you finally arrived back in the United States and set foot on your -- on your native soil, what did you do? What's the first things that you did?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Well, I went -- we landed and went to Indian Town Gap in Pennsylvania, which was an area where they sent the returning solders so they could be released from the Army. And I was released almost immediately, so just glad to be back in the states, because, you know, when you're out of the States, you never know whether you're going to get back or not.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: Looking back at the entire experience from the start -- from start to finish, signing up to finally returning home, would you do anything different?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: No, I definitely wanted to serve in the -- in the service in some degree, because everybody had to do it. As I said, there was a few draft dodgers, but not many that I knew of. So, of course, I would have done it again if I had to. It's just something that you did.

sp.speaker: William Unger
sp.p: All right. Thank you very much. And do you have any final things to say?

sp.speaker: Frank Pipperata
sp.p: Not really. As I say, I was glad that I served and whatever I did toward the war effort. People were involved in the war even in -- civilians were involved in certain ways in defense building, and women got defense jobs and things like -- everybody pulled together. So I was glad I did my part. END OF DISK 1, TRACK 1
